Question: Do agents exist as first-class entities in enterprise identity systems (not service accounts)? Do they have roles, reporting lines, delegated authority, lifecycle states?
Response: Yes. Entra Agent ID (part of Agent 365) establishes agents as first-class identity objects in Microsoft Entra ID — distinct from service accounts. Agent identities appear in directories and admin portals with clear 'Agent' designation. Each agent has: roles (defined via Azure RBAC — Hiring Agent, Finance Agent, Fleet Manager), reporting lines (every agent has a responsible person/sponsor providing oversight), delegated authority (scoped permissions configurable per agent identity), and lifecycle states (Agent 365 manages from creation through active operation to retirement). Our Hosted Agent topology: Hiring Agent (hiring-agent@wpp) with access to HR systems, Finance Agent (finance-agent@wpp) with access to finance systems, Fleet Manager (fleet-manager@wpp) with read-only access to telemetry and state. Each is a distinct first-class entity in WPP's identity infrastructure.
Key Technologies: Entra Agent ID, Agent 365 lifecycle management, Azure RBAC

Question: Can agents inherit authority from human sponsors with configurable approval limits? Is authority auditable, time-bound, and revocable?
Response: Yes. Agent authority is delegated from human sponsors with configurable boundaries. (1) Configurable limits: each agent's permissions are scoped via Entra RBAC and APIM policies — the Hiring Agent can create calendar events OBO the hiring manager but cannot approve budget above a threshold. Autonomy thresholds define what the agent can do autonomously vs what requires human approval. (2) Auditable: every action taken under delegated authority is logged with the agent identity and the sponsoring human's identity (for OBO flows). The action ledger in the workflow state store maintains full attribution. (3) Time-bound: Entra Conditional Access policies can enforce time-bound access. Agent 365 lifecycle management supports temporary agent activations for specific projects. (4) Revocable: agent permissions can be revoked immediately via Entra ID admin — the agent loses tool access in real-time. Agent 365 supports lifecycle actions (activate, block, delete).
Key Technologies: Entra Agent ID, Entra Conditional Access, Agent 365 lifecycle, APIM policies, OBO flows

Question: Does the platform produce audit artefacts to support legal accountability: who authorised the agent, what policy governed the decision, what data was used, what human approved or could override?
Response: Yes. Complete legal audit artefact chain. (1) Who authorised the agent: Agent 365 records the responsible person/sponsor for each agent identity. API Center records who approved each skill promotion. (2) What policy governed the decision: OTEL spans record which skill version was active, which autonomy thresholds applied, and which governance rules were evaluated. APIM logs record which policies were enforced on each tool call. (3) What data was used: OTEL traces capture every MCP tool call with parameters and data sources accessed. Knowledge source bindings are declared in skills and logged at execution. (4) What human approved or could override: the action ledger records all HITL decisions with approver identity. For non-revocable actions, the approval chain is: agent recommends -> hook blocks -> human's PA presents -> human approves -> deterministic execution. Each step is logged. All artefacts flow to Azure Log Analytics with 7-12 year retention (immutability enforced via Azure Storage export with immutability policies), queryable via KQL and exportable for legal proceedings.
Key Technologies: Agent 365 (sponsorship), OTEL traces, APIM logs, action ledger, Azure Log Analytics (immutable 7-12yr)

Question: Are there performance review mechanisms for agents: success rates, error rates, cost efficiency, user satisfaction? Are underperforming agents flagged for retraining or retirement?
Response: Yes. Agent performance is measurable across multiple dimensions. (1) Success rates: Foundry Evaluators track task completion and quality scores per skill. (2) Error rates: OTEL telemetry and APIM metrics capture failure rates per agent per skill. (3) Cost efficiency: APIM token usage and OTEL cost attribution per workflow provide cost-per-task metrics. Tiered model usage cost visible per skill. (4) User satisfaction: human override rates from the action ledger indicate quality — high override rates signal underperformance. The Fleet Manager agent analyses these metrics and flags underperforming skills on the Control Plane with recommended actions: adjust thresholds, revert to previous skill version, increase HITL oversight, or retire the skill. Agent 365 supports lifecycle actions including suspension and retirement for underperforming agents. ROI self-reporting: per-agent type cost/value reports aggregable for executive reporting.
Key Technologies: Foundry Evaluators, OTEL cost attribution, APIM metrics, Fleet Manager (performance analysis), Agent 365 lifecycle
